body:
Perhaps the solution is not to "integrate" keep-alive fetching with the event-loop, runnable tasks, and document lifetime, but rather to clearly dissociate it from those concepts? 

I can imagine re-defining when a task is "runnable", or introducing a new "keep-alive networking" task source, and say that taks from it can always run, and so on(you'd need a separate task-source, since otherwise you'll lose ordering within the networking one). I think that would probably make a clear processing model much less clear, and create more troubles than solutions. 

On the other hand, I can imagine the following:

 Introduce something like the [session-history-event-loop](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/history.html#session-history-event-loop), and the [session-history-traversal-queue](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/history.html#session-history-traversal-queue). For example, [`sendBeacon`](https://w3c.github.io/beacon/#dom-navigator-sendbeacon) could add a "task" to a dedicated queue, with the user-agent processing those tasks fully "in parellel" to anything that goes on on the regular event-loop. Fetches initiated by those tasks would be fully dissociated from a document, and never be cancelled due to a document unloading. 

Re fetch callback tasks running on the event-loop, and in the context of a document, do we really want that to happen in the case of an inactive documents? I think it could give potentially scary "run JS in the background" capabilities to  webpages. I'm currently quite happy that when I navigated away from something, it can't really keep running fetches, let alone run JS callbacks in response to those fetches...
